title: Patent protection can increase agricultural innovation and local profits while raising seed costs and distorting downstream production
source_unit: NBER Working Paper 35735, Flowers of Invention: The Economic Impacts of Patent Rights; crop-specific technology development, plant reproductive-structure exposure, and U.S. county outcomes
geography: United States agricultural crops, counties, firms, and downstream production; plant-biotechnology patent change introduced in 1985

observations.period: 1985 patent-rights change and subsequent crop-specific and county outcomes; NBER paper issued September 2026

denominator.unit: study-defined crops and U.S. counties differentially exposed by crop composition; public abstract count not disclosed

legal_change.value: plant-biotechnology patent protection was introduced in 1985, with exposure varying by crop reproductive structure
legal_change.unit: property-rights policy change and differential exposure

innovation.value: patent protection increased development of novel plant varieties and rapidly increased private-sector research investment
innovation.unit: crop-technology development and private R&D response

spillover_and_yield.value: the change produced positive spillovers in certain non-biological agricultural technologies and increased crop yields

cost_and_distortion.value: patent rights may impose significant costs on technology consumers and distort downstream production; seed spending increased

local_distribution.value: U.S. counties more exposed through crop composition experienced increases in agricultural land values and profits
local_distribution.unit: local economic outcome by policy exposure

downstream_outcome.value: the abstract does not establish farm-level adoption, farmer bargaining power, food prices, consumer welfare, labor, environmental outcomes, or household food security

observations.method: The paper exploits differential exposure created by plant reproductive structures and combines a new crop-specific technology-development dataset with county-level outcomes to estimate the effects of patent protection on innovation, investment, yields, land values, and profits.
observations.uncertainty: The public abstract does not disclose every crop, county, period, identification assumption, estimate, or downstream-production measure. Higher yields and profits do not establish consumer welfare, and seed-cost increases do not by themselves establish net farmer or household loss.
observations.subgroup: Crops with different reproductive structures, private-sector researchers, agricultural technology consumers, farms, and U.S. counties with different crop-composition exposure.
observations.counterinterpretation: Patent protection can fund innovation that would otherwise not occur, and higher seed costs may reflect valuable technology or quality. County land-value and profit gains may be capitalized benefits rather than gains shared by tenants, workers, or consumers.

related_sources.claim: NBER DOI record for Working Paper 35735

boundary: This record closes a legal-rights-to-private-investment, innovation, yield, and local-profit arrow while preserving the cost and power trade-off: patent rights can raise productivity and land values alongside higher seed spending and possible downstream distortions. It does not establish consumer welfare, farm adoption, worker outcomes, or household food security.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: NBER Working Paper 35735 landing page reviewed and retained only as a source-page hash; crop-level data, county data, paper PDF, and model code were not retained.
